clauses.reason: The approving words of Executive Order 6694-A read: "Now, Therefore, I, Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the United States, pursuant to the authority vested in me by Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, approved June 16, 1933, and otherwise, do adopt and approve the report, recommendations, and findings of the Administrator and do order that effective May 14, 1934, unless just cause to the contrary should theretofore be shown, the said Code of Fair Competition be and it is hereby approved;". The approval is to take effect on May 14, 1934 unless just cause to the contrary were shown before then; that is a commencement condition, not an end, and no held record shows just cause shown (the 1944 WPA list records the code as approved). The approval states no period or until-date. The approval was code-dependent: under section 3(b) of the Act the approved provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade or industry, under section 3(c) the district courts could restrain violations, and under section 3(f) a violation was a misdemeanor, so the approval operated only through section 3. Section 2 of S.J. Res. 113, approved June 14, 1935, provides "All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed". The resolution states no effective date other than its approval, so the approval ceased to operate on June 14, 1935. No held record shows this code cancelled or suspended before June 14, 1935. June 16, 1935 is not an end date: section 1 of the same resolution replaced the original two-year expiry of Title I with April 1, 1936, and nothing in the resolution defers section 2. Schechter (May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization, not as an end date.

The first proviso reads: "provided, that if prior to said effective date the Administrator on his own initiative determines that an emergency due to destructive price-cutting, as stated in Article VI, Section 4 of said Code, exists in the trade, the Administrator may thereupon cause to be determined the lowest reasonable cost as set forth in said Section 4 of Article VI and such determination may thereupon be announced to the members of the trade in such manner as the Administrator shall direct but shall not become binding upon such members until the effective date of the Code;". It lets the Administrator, if he finds before the code's effective date (May 14, 1934) that an emergency due to destructive price-cutting exists, have the lowest reasonable cost determined and announced, without binding members until the effective date. The authority is exercisable only "prior to said effective date", so by its own terms it ended when the effective date arrived. The end is recorded as May 14, 1934, the effective date (the last day on which a determination could be made before that date was May 13, 1934). No held record shows a determination made, so the clause is not recorded as exhausted by performance; it lapsed by its terms. A determination, had one been made, would be a different event that this clause does not rest on. The repeal of June 14, 1935 is a later event and not the first end.

The second proviso reads: "and provided further, that in connection with the existence of an emergency duo to destructive price-cutting and the determination of lowest reasonable cost thereunder as stated in Article VI, Section 4 of the Code in order to eliminate unfair competition the Administrator may establish for the period of such emergency a uniform guarantee and warranty applicable to the sale or offering for sale of any products of the trade;". It authorises the Administrator to establish, for the period of an emergency due to destructive price-cutting under Article VI, Section 4 of the code, a uniform guarantee and warranty for the sale of the trade's products. It states no date; its period is that of an emergency that is itself defined by the code, and no held record shows an emergency declared or a warranty established. The authority exists only through the approved code, and section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 repealed the provisions delegating power to approve codes and providing for their enforcement, effective June 14, 1935, so it ceased to operate on that date. June 16, 1935 is not an end date: section 1 of the same resolution replaced the original two-year expiry of Title I with April 1, 1936, and nothing in the resolution defers section 2.

The third proviso reads: "and provided further, that the provisions of

Article VI, Section 2, insofar as they prescribe a waiting period between the filing with the Code Authority or its duly constituted agency and the effective date of revised price-lists, be and they are hereby stayed pending my further orders or the orders of the Administrator;". It stays the waiting-period part of Article VI, Section 2 of the code until the President or the Administrator orders otherwise. The stated end is a contingent event with no date. No held text records such an order, and the held corpus does not include Administrator orders, so the stay is recorded as ending no later than the repeal and not as having ended earlier. The stay modifies a provision of the approved code and has no operation apart from it, so it fell with the approval on June 14, 1935 under section 2 of S.J. Res. 113. A held order lifting the stay before that date would become this clause's first end. June 16, 1935 is not an end date: section 1 of the same resolution replaced the original two-year expiry of Title I with April 1, 1936, and nothing in the resolution defers section 2.

The fourth proviso reads: "and provided further, that within ninety (90) days of the approval of the Code, the Code Authority shall submit recommendations to the Administrator for the purpose of rendering the hour and wage provisions of this Code as consistent as possible with such provisions in codes of related trades.". It directs the Code Authority to submit recommendations to the Administrator within ninety days of the approval of the code to make the code's hour and wage provisions as consistent as possible with those of related trades. The ninety days are a deadline for the report, not an end of the direction; no held record shows the recommendations submitted or when, so the direction is not recorded as exhausted. It is addressed to the Code Authority, a body that exists only under the code, and operates only with the approved code. Section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 repealed the provisions delegating power to approve codes and providing for their enforcement, effective June 14, 1935, so the direction ceased to operate on that date. June 16, 1935 is not an end date: section 1 of the same resolution replaced the original two-year expiry of Title I with April 1, 1936, and nothing in the resolution defers section 2.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 6694-A (May 1, 1934) approves the Code of Fair Competition for the Retail Rubber Tire and Battery Trade under Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act. The held text is the American Presidency Project transcription (grade mirror_transcription, acceptable_as_original false; Common Crawl capture 2025-10-14T06:13:22Z); the standing note applies: original not yet held; replace and re-check quotes when an official copy is retrieved. The order has five commands: the approval effective May 14, 1934, and four provisos (a pre-effective-date determination authority, an emergency warranty authority, a stay pending further order, and a ninety-day recommendation direction). The first end differs between them. Because each command is dependent on the code and no held record shows an earlier end, the first end is the statutory repeal of the code approval and enforcement provisions by section 2 of S.J. Res. 113, effective June 14, 1935. Schechter, decided May 27, 1935, held the section 3 delegation unconstitutional; that is recorded as a validity characterization (void from issuance under then-prevailing doctrine), not as an end date, because the judgment cancelled no approval. The antitrust-exemption proviso of the resolution is not settled by the held text for past action; whatever survives is an accrued effect, not continued operation of the approval.

Res. 113 or in any held source continues the approval or its enforcement after June 14, 1935. No held source shows a prosecution or injunction continued under this approval after that date.
